books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Secession dates verified against the Ordinance of Secession table (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinance_of_Secession), the American Battlefield Trust Civil War timeline (battlefields.org), and Digital History, University of Houston (digitalhistory.uh.edu). Texas adopted its ordinance February 1, 1861, confirmed by popular referendum February 23; Virginia's ordinance was ratified by referendum May 23, 1861.
stimulus.text:
Ordinances of secession, in the order the states adopted them. Seven states seceded before Lincoln's inauguration on March 4, 1861; four more followed after the firing on Fort Sumter.

| State | Date of ordinance |
| South Carolina | December 20, 1860 |
| Mississippi | January 9, 1861 |
| Florida | January 10, 1861 |
| Alabama | January 11, 1861 |
| Georgia | January 19, 1861 |
| Louisiana | January 26, 1861 |
| Texas | February 1, 1861 |
| Virginia | April 17, 1861 |
| Arkansas | May 6, 1861 |
| Tennessee | May 6, 1861 |
| North Carolina | May 20, 1861 |

Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri were slave states that stayed in the Union and are not listed.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A historian studying the table would most likely conclude that the Upper South's decision to secede depended most on

options.text: the election of Lincoln in November 1860.
options.misconception: The Upper South waited five months after the election; the election alone did not move it.

options.text: Lincoln's response to the firing on Fort Sumter.
the failure of the Crittenden Compromise in December.
options.misconception: Background: the Crittenden Compromise failed in January 1861, but the Upper South still waited until April.

options.text: the adoption of the Confederate Constitution in February.
options.misconception: Background: the Confederate Constitution was adopted February 8, but the Upper South did not join for two more months.

rationales.A: The Upper South waited five months after the election; the election alone did not move it.
rationales.B: Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina all seceded after April 12, within weeks of Sumter and the troop call. Background: the Upper South had refused to leave over the election, but coercion — war against fellow Southerners — changed the question.
rationales.C: Background: the Crittenden Compromise failed in January 1861, but the Upper South still waited until April.
rationales.D: Background: the Confederate Constitution was adopted February 8, but the Upper South did not join for two more months.
rationales.general:
1. The Upper South's dates all fall after April 12.
2. Nothing in the winter moved them; something in April did.
3. Background: Virginia voted to secede April 17, two days after Lincoln's call for 75,000 men.
4. Timing is evidence: when the dates pile up after one event, that event is the cause.
Remember: a cluster of dates after a single event is the strongest timing argument a table can give you.
